newsitem.title: EGYPT: World Bank upbeat on Mideast growth prospects.
newsitem.headline: World Bank upbeat on Mideast growth prospects.

text.p: The World Bank said on Thursday the Middle East and North Africa could achieve annual economic growth of up to six percent if reforms continued to gain speed.
"It would be less than frank to deny that we meet today at a time of some political uncertainty in the region," World Bank Vice President Kemal Dervis told a Cairo economic conference.

"But it would equally be less than fair to deny that we are meeting at a time when the countries of the region, notably including our host country today, Egypt, are beginning to make real progress in creating an economically New Middle East and North Africa."

Dervis said regional efforts to put in place "far-reaching programmes of economic reforms" and increasing integration into the global economy made "an average six percent growth rate...a challenging but feasible target over the next 15 years".
He estimated average GDP growth in the area at more than four percent in 1994 to 1996.

Touting a theme that has underlined discussions at the third annual Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference, Dervis stressed the need for privatisation as a tool to attract foreign investment.

"The role of government will need redefinition away from being a substantial producer of goods and services...towards becoming an effective promotor and referee of private sector oriented growth and private investment," he said.

Host country Egypt has highlighted at the conference its ambitious privatisation programme, in which it has sold off a majority stake in about a dozen companies this year and plans to sell equity in 91 companies in the next 18 months.

The conference, the third since Israel and the Palestinians signed an interim peace deal in 1993, has concentrated on pressing the internal economic reforms business people say the region needs to catch up with the rest of the world.

Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor, attending the meeting which Egypt almost cancelled in anger at right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, said the Jewish state's delegation would "go home quite satisfied".

"The real business result of the conference, in contracts eventually being signed, of course will be known somewhat later when we gather with our business people and hear from them," Meridor told a news conference.

"In spite of some early remarks which were not very welcoming to Israel, the reality we found here in the halls, in the corridors, in the meetings was very positive, both from the political element and from the economic element," he said.

On Wednesday -- in a direct snub to Israel -- Egypt, Turkey and the U.S. oil company Amoco signed an agreement for Egypt to export to Turkey up to 10 billion cubic metres of liquefied natural gas a year by the year 2000. This replaces a project for a "peace pipeline" which was to have run through Israel.

In a speech to the conference on Thursday, Palestinian minister Nabil Shaath said the Palestinian Authority would ask donors for $800 million towards its public investment programme for 1997 at a consultative group meeting in Paris next week.
The Authority, which runs parts of the Gaza Strip and West Bank, has increased the portion of that allocated to private sector development to 20 percent from six percent this year, he said.

Shaath, minister of economic planning and international cooperation, did not give a figure for this year's public investment programme but said donors had disbursed about $1 billion of the $3 billion they had pledged since 1993.
